title: Baptism
summary: Baptism is a new covenant practice that marks initiation, remembrance, and communal identity in the church.
historical_context: Baptism appears in the New Testament as the church reflects on Jesus' saving work and the shape of the community.
ancient_near_east_context: Ritual washing, meal fellowship, and covenant renewal provide the wider background.
literary_context: Gospels and epistles use Baptism to connect Jesus' work to church practice.
covenantal_significance: Baptism signals that the people of God now live in the fulfillment of the covenant in Christ.

interpretive_notes.note: New covenant institutions are both theological signs and communal practices.
Their meaning comes from Jesus and the apostolic witness, not later tradition alone.

common_questions: How does this institution work in the New Testament?
Why is this practice important for the church?
What new covenant theme does this institution express?
hebraic_worldview: Baptism belongs to purification, repentance, and new-identity language before later sacramental debates.
second_temple_context: Purification washings, John the Baptist, and repentance shape the backdrop of baptism in the Gospels and Acts.
canonical_context: Baptism gathers creation, flood, exodus, and Spirit themes into a rite of new identity in Christ.
later_christian_reception: Christian traditions have debated baptism's mode and effect, but it must stay grounded in its Jewish and apostolic setting.
